cards.title: Introduction to Exceptions
cards.content:
What is an Exception?

An exception is an event that disrupts the normal flow of a program's execution. It is an object wrapped around an error event that occurred within a method.

In Java, all exception and error types are subclasses of the Throwable class, which is the root of the exception hierarchy.

// A simple example of exceptional behavior
int result = 10 / 0; // Throws ArithmeticException

cards.title: Checked vs. Unchecked Exceptions
cards.content:
The Two Main Branches

Exceptions in Java are categorized into two major categories:

  • Checked Exceptions: Checked at compile-time. The compiler forces you to handle them using try-catch or declare them using throws. Examples: IOException, SQLException.
  • Unchecked Exceptions (Runtime Exceptions): Checked at runtime. They extend RuntimeException and usually result from programming logic errors. Examples: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

options.text: NullPointerException is checked; IOException is unchecked.
NullPointerException is unchecked; IOException is checked.
Both are checked exceptions enforced by the compiler.
Both are unchecked exceptions occurring during runtime.

cards.title: The Try-Catch-Finally Block
cards.content:
Handling Exceptions gracefully

We handle exceptions using the try, catch, and finally blocks.

  • try: Guards the block of code where exceptions might occur.
  • catch: Executes only if an exception of the matching type occurs in the try block.
  • finally: Always executes, regardless of whether an exception was thrown or caught. Ideal for cleaning up system resources.

cards.title: Try-With-Resources
cards.content:
Automatic Resource Management

Introduced in Java 7, try-with-resources simplifies resource management by automatically closing resources declared in the try statement.

Any resource that implements the java.lang.AutoCloseable interface can be used in this construct.

try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("test.txt"))) {
    System.out.println(br.readLine());
} catch (IOException e) {
    e.printStackTrace();
} // br is automatically closed here

items.text: Code inside the try block starts executing sequentially.
An exception is thrown at a specific line in the try block.
The rest of the try block is skipped, and execution moves to the matching catch block.
The code inside the catch block completes execution.

cards.title: Throw vs. Throws
cards.content:
Throw vs Throws

While they sound identical, they serve completely different tasks:

  • throw: Explicitly throws a single exception instance from your code. (e.g., throw new IllegalArgumentException();)
  • throws: Declared in a method signature to specify that this method can potentially throw these exceptions to its callers. (e.g., public void read() throws IOException)

right.text: Attempting to divide an integer by zero.
Invoking a method on an object reference that is null.
Accessing index 5 on an array of size 3.
Attempting to open a file that does not exist on disk.

cards.title: Custom Exceptions
cards.content:
Creating User-Defined Exceptions

Sometimes, Java's built-in exceptions cannot express specific business domain logic. In such cases, you can build custom exceptions.

  • To make a checked exception: Extend Exception.
  • To make an unchecked exception: Extend RuntimeException.
public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {
    public InsufficientFundsException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}

options.text: Always catch the base Exception class directly to handle any potential error in one block.
Catch specific subclasses of exceptions first, then general ones if necessary.
Leave catch blocks completely empty to ignore non-critical errors.
Use exceptions as normal logic statements instead of if/else conditions.
